title: Darwin and FitzRoy Aboard the Beagle
text:
In 1831 Captain Robert FitzRoy, twenty six years old, was preparing HMS Beagle for a long survey voyage around South America. Commanding a ship meant isolation, and FitzRoy wanted a gentleman companion to share his meals and conversation. The post went to Charles Darwin, a twenty two year old graduate with a passion for natural history. The voyage lasted almost five years.

The two lived at close quarters and admired each other, but they also clashed. FitzRoy had a fierce temper. Darwin later recalled a quarrel in Brazil over slavery: FitzRoy said slaves he had asked had told him they were happy, and Darwin asked what such an answer was worth in front of their master. FitzRoy exploded and said they could not live together. Within hours he apologized.

After the voyage their paths split. Darwin's observations led him to evolution. FitzRoy, a devout believer, came to regret that his ship had carried the man who wrote On the Origin of Species, and spoke against it. He went on to found official weather forecasting in Britain. Worn down by overwork and disappointment, he took his own life in 1865. Darwin contributed to a fund for his family.
lesson: Close companions can drift apart when their beliefs collide. Disagreement need not erase gratitude for what you shared.
location: HMS Beagle, South America, and England
source: Charles Darwin, Journal of Researches (The Voyage of the Beagle, 1839); Darwin, Autobiography; Darwin's correspondence
